hook.text: An iPhone: designed in California, chips from Taiwan, assembled in China, sold in 175 countries. That's global ops.

buildup.text: Companies go global to access cheaper labor, larger markets, specialized skills, and natural resources.

discovery.text: Global operations let firms produce where costs are lowest and sell where demand is highest—arbitraging the world.

twist.text: Going global adds complexity: time zones, languages, regulations, and logistics that domestic operations never face.

climax.text: The most successful global firms balance cost advantage with the complexity cost of managing across borders.

punchline.text: Global ops offer huge gains—and huge complexity.

quiz.question: Why do companies globalize operations?
options: To access cheaper labor and larger markets

hook.text: Nike doesn't own a single factory. It outsources everything. Apple offshores to Foxconn. The difference matters.

buildup.text: Offshoring moves your own operations to another country. Outsourcing hands operations to an external company.

discovery.text: You can offshore without outsourcing (your factory abroad) or outsource without offshoring (local contractor).

twist.text: Many companies offshore and outsource simultaneously—hiring a foreign contractor—getting both benefits and both risks.

climax.text: The choice depends on control needs, cost targets, intellectual property risk, and available capabilities.

punchline.text: Know whether you're moving the work or giving it away.

quiz.question: What is offshoring?
options: Moving your operations to another country

hook.text: Bangladesh makes T-shirts. Switzerland makes watches. Each focuses on what it does best. That's comparative advantage.

buildup.text: David Ricardo's 1817 theory says countries benefit by specializing in goods they produce at the lowest opportunity cost.

discovery.text: Even if one country is better at everything, both gain by specializing and trading. Relative cost matters, not absolute.

twist.text: Comparative advantage shifts over time. China moved from textiles to electronics to AI as its workforce skills grew.

climax.text: Global operations exploit comparative advantage—sourcing each component from the most efficient location.

punchline.text: Make what you're relatively best at. Trade for the rest.

quiz.question: What does comparative advantage suggest?
options: Specialize in goods with the lowest opportunity cost

hook.text: Starbucks has 35,000 stores in 80 countries. It didn't just export coffee—it adapted operations for every market.

buildup.text: Companies enter global markets through exporting, licensing, joint ventures, or wholly-owned subsidiaries.

discovery.text: Each mode trades off control, risk, and speed. Exporting is low-risk; full ownership is high-risk but high-control.

twist.text: McDonald's uses franchising in most countries but owns outlets in key markets—the entry mode matches the strategic need.

climax.text: The best global firms use different entry modes in different markets—one size never fits all.

punchline.text: Enter each market the way that market demands.

quiz.question: Why do companies use different entry modes in different markets?
options: Each market has different risks and opportunities

hook.text: IKEA sells the same furniture worldwide. McDonald's sells rice burgers in Japan. Standardize or localize? Both cost.

buildup.text: Global standardization reduces cost through scale. Local adaptation increases relevance to each market.

discovery.text: The integration-responsiveness framework maps the tension: integration favors global, responsiveness favors local.

twist.text: Most firms need both—a global platform with local tweaks. The trick is deciding what to standardize and what to adapt.

climax.text: Toyota uses global platforms but adjusts features, pricing, and marketing by region—glocal operations.

punchline.text: Think global. Act local. Design for both.

quiz.question: What is the glocal approach?

hook.text: Zara's network spans 12 countries, 1,600 suppliers, and delivers new fashion in 15 days. Network design is strategy.

buildup.text: Global network design decides where to locate factories, warehouses, and suppliers to serve worldwide demand.

discovery.text: Decisions include number and location of facilities, capacity allocation, and which products to make where.

twist.text: Network design locks in costs and capabilities for years. A bad location choice can't be fixed with better management.

climax.text: Amazon redesigns its network annually—adding fulfillment centers where demand grows fastest. Agility is the new normal.

punchline.text: Where you put your operations defines what they can deliver.

quiz.question: Why is global network design a long-term decision?
options: Facility locations lock in costs for years

hook.text: A European car has parts from 30 countries. Global sourcing finds the best supplier worldwide—not just nearby.

buildup.text: Global sourcing means picking suppliers from anywhere in the world based on cost, quality, capability, and reliability.

discovery.text: It provides access to specialized capabilities, lower costs, and materials unavailable domestically.

twist.text: Longer distances mean longer lead times, higher shipping costs, and more risk from disruptions and currency changes.

climax.text: Companies increasingly use total landed cost—not just unit price—to compare domestic and global suppliers fairly.

punchline.text: Buy globally but calculate the total cost, not just the price.

quiz.question: What should companies use to compare global suppliers?

hook.text: A factory in a free trade zone imports materials duty-free and exports finished goods tariff-free. It's a tax island.

buildup.text: Free trade zones are designated areas where goods are imported, stored, and processed without standard customs duties.

discovery.text: Companies use FTZs to defer duties, reduce paperwork, and lower costs on goods destined for re-export.

twist.text: FTZs can distort location decisions—companies choose sites for tax benefits rather than operational efficiency.

climax.text: China's Shenzhen Special Economic Zone transformed from a fishing village to a tech powerhouse using FTZ incentives.

punchline.text: Free trade zones lower costs—if you plan around them.

quiz.question: What is a free trade zone?
options: An area where goods move without standard duties

hook.text: Singapore, Dubai, and Rotterdam handle goods for continents. One port city can be the gateway to a billion customers.

buildup.text: Logistics hubs are strategic locations where transportation modes converge—sea, air, rail, and road.

discovery.text: Companies position distribution centers near hubs to reach multiple markets quickly with lower shipping costs.

twist.text: Over-reliance on one hub creates concentration risk. When the Suez was blocked, hubs on that route were paralyzed.

climax.text: Dubai turned logistics into a national strategy—its port and airport handle cargo for Africa, Asia, and Europe.

punchline.text: Location near a hub turns geography into advantage.

quiz.question: Why do companies locate near logistics hubs?

hook.text: A company sells parts from its Irish subsidiary to its US parent at a price that shifts profit to the lower-tax country.

buildup.text: Transfer pricing is the price charged between divisions of the same company for goods or services moving across borders.

discovery.text: Companies use transfer pricing to allocate profits to lower-tax jurisdictions—legally reducing their global tax bill.

twist.text: Governments fight aggressive transfer pricing. The OECD's arm's-length principle says prices must match market rates.

climax.text: Apple faced a $14 billion EU tax ruling for routing profits through Ireland. Transfer pricing is under global scrutiny.

punchline.text: Move products across borders. Profits follow—and so do regulators.

quiz.question: What is transfer pricing?
options: Prices charged between divisions of the same company

hook.text: A 25% tariff on steel doubled the cost of imported metal overnight. Manufacturers scrambled to find alternatives.

buildup.text: Tariffs are import taxes that raise prices for foreign goods. They protect domestic producers but raise buyer costs.

discovery.text: Non-tariff barriers include quotas, regulations, standards, and red tape—equally powerful at restricting trade.

twist.text: Tariffs intended to protect domestic jobs sometimes destroy more jobs downstream than they save upstream.

climax.text: The US-China trade war showed how tariff escalation disrupts supply chains, raises prices, and creates uncertainty.

punchline.text: Tariffs protect some and hurt others. The net effect is debated endlessly.

quiz.question: What is a non-tariff trade barrier?
options: Regulations or quotas that restrict imports

hook.text: NAFTA turned North America into one of the world's largest free trade zones. Factories relocated within months.

buildup.text: Trade agreements reduce tariffs and harmonize regulations between member countries, enabling freer movement of goods.

discovery.text: They create rules of origin that determine which goods qualify for preferential treatment based on where value is added.

twist.text: Trade agreements have winners and losers. Workers in industries facing new competition often bear the adjustment cost.

climax.text: USMCA replaced NAFTA with updated rules on digital trade, labor standards, and automotive content requirements.

punchline.text: Trade deals open borders for goods. Companies must adapt or lose.

quiz.question: What do trade agreements typically reduce?

hook.text: The US banned advanced chip exports to China. NVIDIA lost billions overnight. Geopolitics reshapes supply chains.

buildup.text: Export controls restrict selling certain technologies or products to specific countries for national security reasons.

discovery.text: Sanctions are broader: they can ban all trade, freeze assets, and cut off financial transactions with targeted nations.

twist.text: Firms must screen every deal against sanctions lists. One violation can trigger massive fines and criminal charges.

climax.text: Semiconductor export restrictions are reshaping global tech supply chains as companies redesign around new boundaries.

punchline.text: What you can sell depends on who you sell it to.

quiz.question: What do export controls restrict?
options: Selling certain technologies to specific countries

hook.text: A toy legal in the US is banned in Europe because of a chemical in the paint. Same product, different rules.

buildup.text: Every country has its own product safety, environmental, labeling, and import regulations that companies must follow.

discovery.text: Compliance costs include testing, certification, documentation, reformulation, and sometimes separate product versions.

twist.text: Non-compliance doesn't just mean fines—products can be seized at the border, destroyed, or trigger consumer lawsuits.

climax.text: The EU's CE marking, REACH regulations, and GDPR create a compliance web that every global operator must navigate.

punchline.text: Global products need local compliance. No exceptions.

quiz.question: What happens if products don't meet a country's regulations?
options: They can be seized or destroyed at the border

hook.text: A US company signs a contract in euros. The dollar weakens 10%. That contract now costs 10% more than planned.

buildup.text: Currency fluctuations change the real cost of imported materials, exported goods, and overseas profits.

discovery.text: Companies manage currency risk through hedging, natural hedging, and pricing strategies that pass risk to customers.

twist.text: Even hedging has limits. Long-term currency shifts can make an entire sourcing strategy uneconomical.

climax.text: Toyota builds factories in its major markets. Producing locally in local currency is the ultimate natural hedge.

punchline.text: Currencies move. Plan for it or pay for it.

quiz.question: What is natural hedging?
options: Producing locally in the same currency as sales

hook.text: A US manager asks a Japanese supplier if a deadline is realistic. They say yes—meaning it's impossible. Culture gap.

buildup.text: High-context cultures like Japan communicate indirectly. Low-context cultures like the US communicate explicitly.

discovery.text: Misunderstanding indirect communication leads to missed deadlines, quality issues, and broken trust between partners.

twist.text: Email makes it worse—tone and context are lost. A message meant as polite can read as demanding across cultures.

climax.text: Companies that train managers in cross-cultural communication reduce costly misunderstandings by up to 50%.

punchline.text: What's said isn't always what's meant. Learn the culture.

quiz.question: What is a high-context culture?
options: One that uses only written communication
One that communicates indirectly with implied meaning

hook.text: A team spans San Francisco, Berlin, and Bangalore. When California wakes up, India is going to bed. Coordination is key.

buildup.text: Global teams offer diverse perspectives but face challenges: time zones, languages, and different work norms.

discovery.text: Effective global teams establish shared rituals, overlapping hours, and documentation-first communication.

twist.text: Trust is harder to build remotely and across cultures. Without it, misunderstandings escalate into conflict fast.

climax.text: Companies that invest in periodic in-person meetups for global teams report 30% higher collaboration scores.

punchline.text: Global teams need global effort—in time, trust, and tools.

quiz.question: What helps global teams build trust?
options: Working only in one time zone

hook.text: A factory in Country A pays workers $2/day with 14-hour shifts. In Country B, that's illegal. Who sets the standard?

buildup.text: Labor standards vary wildly: minimum wage, working hours, child labor laws, and safety regulations differ by country.

discovery.text: The ILO sets international labor standards, but enforcement depends entirely on national governments.

twist.text: Companies sourcing from low-standard countries face reputational risk even if they follow local laws.

climax.text: Nike's 1990s sweatshop scandal showed that customers hold brands responsible for supplier labor practices.

punchline.text: Legal doesn't mean ethical. The market judges both.

quiz.question: Who sets international labor standards?

hook.text: In some cultures, questioning your boss is brave. In others, it's career suicide. Hofstede measured these differences.

buildup.text: Geert Hofstede studied IBM employees across 70 countries and identified six dimensions of national culture.

discovery.text: Dimensions include power distance, individualism, uncertainty avoidance, masculinity, long-term focus, and indulgence.

twist.text: High power distance cultures accept hierarchy. Low power distance cultures expect equality. Managing both is tricky.

climax.text: Operations managers use Hofstede's framework to adapt leadership, communication, and decision-making styles by country.

punchline.text: Culture shapes how people work. Understand it or clash with it.

quiz.question: What does power distance measure?

hook.text: A bribe to a customs official clears your shipment in hours, not weeks. Ethical? Illegal? Many firms face this daily.

buildup.text: Corruption adds unpredictable costs and risks to global operations—bribes, kickbacks, and facilitation payments.

discovery.text: The US Foreign Corrupt Practices Act and UK Bribery Act criminalize bribery abroad—even if it's common locally.

twist.text: Refusing bribes can cost contracts and slow operations. But paying them risks criminal prosecution and reputation.

climax.text: Transparent operations, strong compliance programs, and local partners with integrity are the best defenses.

punchline.text: Integrity is expensive short-term. Corruption is expensive long-term.

quiz.question: What law criminalizes US companies bribing foreign officials?

hook.text: A coup d'état in a country where you source 40% of your materials. By morning, your supply chain is cut off.

buildup.text: Political instability includes regime changes, civil unrest, policy reversals, and asset nationalization.

discovery.text: Companies assess political risk using country risk scores that rate governance, stability, and rule of law.

twist.text: Stable countries can become unstable quickly. Risk scores are lagging indicators—they reflect the past, not the future.

climax.text: Firms operating in high-risk regions use political risk insurance and maintain alternative sourcing plans.

punchline.text: Governments change. Supply chains must survive the change.

quiz.question: What is political risk insurance?
options: Coverage against losses from political events

hook.text: Japan's 2011 tsunami halted auto production worldwide. A 9.0 quake in one country froze factories on every continent.

buildup.text: Natural disasters—earthquakes, floods, hurricanes, volcanoes—can destroy facilities and block transportation routes.

discovery.text: Global chains amplify the impact: a disruption in one location cascades through interconnected supply networks.

twist.text: Companies often don't know they're exposed until disaster hits. Sub-tier suppliers in risk zones are invisible.

climax.text: After 2011, Toyota mapped its supply chain 10 tiers deep and built inventory buffers for critical components.

punchline.text: Map your risk before nature maps it for you.

quiz.question: What did Toyota do after the 2011 tsunami?
options: Mapped its supply chain 10 tiers deep

hook.text: COVID-19 closed factories across Asia in weeks. Months later, the ripple reached every store shelf on Earth.

buildup.text: Pandemics disrupt labor availability, transportation, and demand simultaneously—a triple shock to supply chains.

discovery.text: COVID exposed dependence on single-country sourcing, just-in-time fragility, and lack of supply chain visibility.

twist.text: Some products surged—masks, sanitizer, home office gear—while others collapsed. Agile firms pivoted; rigid firms froze.

climax.text: Post-COVID, companies are building regionalized supply chains, safety stock buffers, and digital visibility tools.

punchline.text: The next pandemic is a matter of when, not if. Prepare now.

quiz.question: What did COVID expose about global supply chains?

hook.text: The NotPetya cyberattack shut down Maersk's shipping operations for two weeks. Global trade lost $10 billion.

buildup.text: Global operations depend on interconnected IT systems. A cyberattack on one node can cascade through the entire network.

discovery.text: Ransomware, data breaches, and system disruptions can halt production, logistics, and financial transactions.

twist.text: Attackers target the weakest link—often a small supplier with minimal security protecting access to the larger network.

climax.text: Companies now require cyber standards from suppliers and segment networks so a breach in one area doesn't spread.

punchline.text: Your security is only as strong as your weakest partner's.

quiz.question: Why do cyberattackers target small suppliers?

hook.text: A firm shares designs with a Chinese factory. Years later, a near-identical product appears under a different brand.

buildup.text: Going global means sharing designs, processes, and technology with partners in countries with varying IP protections.

discovery.text: IP risks include counterfeiting, reverse engineering, employee poaching, and outright theft of trade secrets.

twist.text: Legal protections exist but enforcement varies enormously. A patent in one country means nothing in another.

climax.text: Companies protect IP through contracts, compartmentalized knowledge, and keeping core technology in-house.

punchline.text: Share enough to collaborate. Protect enough to compete.

quiz.question: How do companies protect IP in global operations?
options: Contracts and keeping core technology in-house

hook.text: After decades of offshoring, firms bring factories home. The cheap-labor advantage is shrinking. Reshoring is rising.

buildup.text: Reshoring means moving operations back to the home country after previously offshoring them.

discovery.text: Drivers: rising overseas wages, automation cutting domestic labor costs, supply chain risk, and demand for local goods.

twist.text: Reshoring isn't free—rebuilding domestic supply bases takes years and the skilled workforce may no longer exist.

climax.text: The US CHIPS Act offers $52 billion to reshore semiconductor manufacturing. Government policy is accelerating the trend.

punchline.text: Reshoring is strategic, not nostalgic. The math is changing.

quiz.question: What is driving the reshoring movement?
options: Rising overseas wages and supply chain risk

hook.text: Instead of shipping from China, a US firm moves production to Mexico. Same time zone, shorter supply chain, lower risk.

buildup.text: Nearshoring moves operations to nearby countries—close enough for short lead times but cheap enough for cost savings.

discovery.text: Mexico, Eastern Europe, and Turkey have become nearshoring hubs for the US, Western Europe, and the Middle East.

twist.text: Nearshoring isn't always cheaper than offshoring. The value is in shorter lead times, easier visits, and reduced risk.

climax.text: Mexico surpassed China as the top US import source in 2023—nearshoring is reshaping global trade patterns.

punchline.text: Close enough to visit. Far enough to save.

quiz.question: Why is Mexico becoming a nearshoring hub for the US?

hook.text: A robot works 24/7 for $8/hour fully loaded. A factory worker in China earns $6/hour. The gap is closing fast.

buildup.text: Automation is making labor cost less relevant in location decisions. If robots do the work, cheap labor doesn't matter.

discovery.text: As robot costs fall 20% per year, the economic case for offshoring to low-wage countries weakens.

twist.text: Automation reshoring works for standardized products. Complex, low-volume items still need skilled manual labor abroad.

climax.text: Adidas opened fully automated Speedfactories in Germany and the US—bringing shoe production home through robotics.

punchline.text: When robots are cheaper than workers, location follows customers.

quiz.question: How does automation affect reshoring?
options: It reduces the importance of labor cost in location decisions

hook.text: Instead of one global supply chain, companies now build three: one for the Americas, one for Europe, one for Asia.

buildup.text: Regionalization creates self-contained supply chains within major trade blocs, reducing cross-continental dependency.

discovery.text: Each regional chain sources, makes, and distributes locally—shortening lead times and reducing geopolitical exposure.

twist.text: Regionalization sacrifices some scale economies. Three smaller networks cost more than one optimized global network.

climax.text: Post-COVID, companies like Toyota, Samsung, and Apple are building redundant regional supply chains for resilience.

punchline.text: Three smaller chains may be safer than one giant one.

quiz.question: What does supply chain regionalization sacrifice?

hook.text: Global operations won't disappear. But they're being redesigned for resilience, not just efficiency.

buildup.text: The era of pure cost arbitrage is fading. Companies now optimize for a mix of cost, risk, speed, and sustainability.

discovery.text: Digital tools—AI, digital twins, IoT—let firms manage complex global networks with visibility never possible before.

twist.text: The next disruption is already forming. Companies that survive will be those that built flexibility into their networks.

climax.text: The winning formula: global reach, regional resilience, digital visibility, and agility to pivot when the world shifts.

punchline.text: Global is forever. Fragile is not. Build for both.

quiz.question: What are companies optimizing global operations for now?
options: A mix of cost, risk, speed, and sustainability
